title: The Moon Who Wanted a Nap
paragraphs: High above a quiet town, the Moon had worked all night long. She had lit the rooftops. She had lit the sleepy fields. She had even lit the path for a little lost owl.
"I am so tired," said the Moon with a big, round yawn. "I would like a nap. But who will light the sky while I sleep?"
A small star blinked beside her. "We can help," said the star. "There are many of us. If we all shine a little brighter, the sky will stay bright enough."
The Moon was not sure. "You are very small," she said.
"Small things can do big jobs when they work together," said the star.
So the star called to her friends. One by one, the stars began to glow. A few shone near the hills. A few shone over the lake. Soon the whole sky sparkled like a blanket full of tiny lights.
Down below, the little owl looked up. "What a pretty sky," she hooted. She found her way home and tucked her head under her wing.
The Moon smiled. She pulled a soft gray cloud over herself like a quilt. "Thank you, stars," she whispered.
"Sleep well, Moon," the stars whispered back.
And all night long, the stars kept the sky bright, while the Moon had the coziest nap she had ever had. When morning came, the Sun peeked over the hills and saw the stars still twinkling.
"Good job, everyone," said the Sun. "Now it is your turn to rest."
So the stars closed their eyes, the Moon woke up rested and happy, and the whole sky said good night.

title: Pip and the Missing Mitten
paragraphs: Pip was a little gray mouse who lived inside a garden wall. One snowy morning, Pip found something red and soft lying in the snow. It was a mitten, warm and fuzzy and much too big for a mouse.
"Someone must be missing this," said Pip. "I will find them."
Pip carried the mitten to the rabbit. "Is this yours?" asked Pip.
"No," said the rabbit. "My paws stay warm in my fur. But I saw a girl building a snowman by the gate."
Pip carried the mitten to the gate. The snowman was there, with a carrot nose and two button eyes. But the girl was gone.
Pip sat down in the snow. The mitten was heavy, and Pip was cold. "Maybe I will just sleep inside it for a little while," Pip thought.
Pip crawled into the mitten. It was like a tiny red tent. It was so warm that Pip fell fast asleep.
Soon, footsteps crunched in the snow. A girl in a striped hat bent down. "My mitten!" she said. She picked it up, and out popped a sleepy little mouse.
The girl laughed softly. "Were you keeping my mitten warm for me?"
Pip nodded, because that was almost true.
The girl smiled. She put the mitten on and held out her other hand. In it was a crumb of cookie. "Thank you, little friend," she said.
Pip took the crumb and ran home to the garden wall. That night, Pip snuggled into a bed of soft moss, still a little warm, and dreamed of red mittens and kind friends.

title: The Lighthouse Cat
paragraphs: At the edge of a rocky island stood a tall white lighthouse. At the very top, next to the big glass lamp, lived a cat named Juniper. Juniper had soft orange fur and one white paw, and she had the most important job on the island.

Every evening, when the sky turned pink, Juniper climbed the winding stairs. One, two, three, all the way to one hundred. At the top, she sat beside the keeper while he turned on the great lamp. Then the light swept around and around, across the dark water, so the boats would know where the rocks were.
One night, a thick fog rolled in. It was so thick that Juniper could not see the water at all. The keeper frowned. "The light can't reach very far tonight," he said. "I hope the boats stay safe."
Juniper pressed her nose to the glass. Far out in the fog, she heard a sound. Ding. Ding. It was the little bell on the fishing boat that belonged to Mrs. Alvarez. The bell sounded lost.

Juniper had an idea. She ran down all one hundred stairs, out the door, and onto the rocks. Then she found the old brass bell that hung by the dock, the one nobody used anymore. Juniper reached up with her white paw and batted the rope.
Clang! Clang! The big bell rang out over the water.
The keeper hurried down the stairs. "Juniper, what are you doing?" Then he heard the little bell answer. Ding. Ding. It was getting closer.

"She's following the sound!" said the keeper. He took the rope and rang the big bell again and again. Clang! Clang! Ding! Ding! Slowly, out of the fog, came a small blue boat. Mrs. Alvarez waved from the deck.
"I couldn't see the light," she called, "but I could hear your bell! Thank you!"
The keeper scooped Juniper up and scratched behind her ears. "You found a new way to keep the boats safe," he said. "The light helps them see, and the bell helps them hear."
From then on, whenever the fog came, the keeper rang the brass bell, and Juniper sat beside him, listening for little bells answering in the night.

When the fog finally drifted away, the stars came out over the calm sea. Juniper climbed back up the hundred stairs, curled up beside the warm lamp, and purred herself to sleep while the light went around and around.

title: Benny Builds a Bridge
paragraphs: Benny was a young beaver who loved to build. He built tiny houses out of twigs. He built towers out of pebbles. He even built a little boat out of a leaf, though it only floated for a moment before it sank.
One spring morning, Benny heard a squeaky voice by the creek. It was Hazel the hedgehog. She was standing on one side of the water, looking at the other side.
"What's wrong?" asked Benny.
"My grandma lives across the creek," said Hazel. "I made her a basket of berries. But the stepping stones washed away in the rain, and I can't swim."
Benny looked at the creek. It was too wide to jump. It was too fast to wade. "I can build you a bridge!" he said.
Benny got to work. He chewed a long, straight branch and pushed it across the water. But when Hazel stepped on it, it rolled and wobbled. She jumped back just in time.
"Hmm," said Benny. "One branch is not enough."

He chewed another branch and laid it next to the first one. Then another, and another. He tied them together with long strips of soft bark. Now the bridge was wide and flat. But when Hazel stepped on it, it sagged in the middle and touched the water.
"Hmm," said Benny again. He did not give up. He found two big rocks and rolled them into the middle of the creek. Then he set the bridge on top of the rocks, so it had something to rest on.
"Try it now," said Benny.

Hazel took one careful step. Then another. The bridge did not roll. It did not sag. It held steady all the way across. "It works!" she cheered. She hurried to her grandma's house, holding her basket of berries high.

That evening, Hazel's grandma came back across the bridge with Hazel to say thank you. She brought Benny a warm acorn muffin. "This is a fine bridge," she said. "Now the whole forest can visit each other."
Soon, rabbits hopped across it. Squirrels scampered across it. A family of ducks waddled across it, quacking happily. Benny watched them all, feeling proud.
"My first bridge rolled, and my second bridge sagged," he told Hazel. "But the third one was just right."
"That's because you kept trying," said Hazel.
That night, Benny curled up in his cozy lodge, listening to the creek bubble past his bridge. He was already dreaming about what he might build tomorrow.

title: The Kite That Wanted to See the World
paragraphs: In a little house at the bottom of a green hill, there lived a kite named Skye. Skye was shaped like a diamond, with yellow and blue stripes and a long tail made of ribbons. Most days, Skye hung on a hook in the hallway, waiting for a windy afternoon.

When the wind finally came, the girl who owned Skye would carry her up the hill. She would let out the string, and Skye would rise up, up, up into the sky. From way up high, Skye could see the whole town. She could see the red barn, the blue pond and the road that curled away over the hills.
"I wonder what is past those hills," Skye said to the wind one day.
"Many things," said the wind. "Mountains and rivers and cities and seas."
"I wish I could see them," sighed Skye. "But my string only goes so far."
The wind was quiet for a moment. Then it said, "I travel everywhere. Every night I will come to your window and tell you what I saw."
That night, the wind tapped on the hallway window. Skye listened from her hook.
"Today I blew across a mountain so tall that it wore a hat of snow," said the wind. "A family of goats climbed its rocky sides, and the smallest goat jumped from stone to stone like he was dancing."
Skye closed her eyes and pictured the mountain. She could almost feel the cold air.

The next night, the wind came again. "Today I rippled across a wide river," it said. "A heron stood very still in the shallow water, waiting for a fish. When the sun went down, the whole river turned gold."
Skye smiled. She could almost see the golden water.

Night after night, the wind told her stories. It told her about a city full of lights, where people walked their dogs on busy sidewalks. It told her about a desert where the sand made little waves, just like the sea. It told her about a sea so big that it seemed to go on forever, with whales spouting far away.
One evening, the wind did not come. Skye waited and waited. The window was quiet. She began to worry. "What if the wind forgot about me?" she thought.
The next morning, the girl took Skye up the hill. The air was very still. Skye flopped on the grass. She could not fly at all.
"Where are you, wind?" Skye whispered.
Then, far away, the trees began to sway. The grass began to ripple. And the wind came rushing up the hill, a little out of breath.
"I'm sorry I was late," said the wind. "I went farther than ever before. I went all the way around the world, and I brought you something."
The wind swirled, and something landed gently on Skye's tail. It was a single white feather.
"It's from a seabird I met on the far side of the ocean," said the wind. "She asked me to tell you that even a kite on a string can know the whole world, if she listens to its stories."

Skye felt warm all over. She lifted into the air, higher than she ever had before, with the white feather fluttering on her tail. From up high, she looked at the hills, and she did not feel sad about what was past them anymore. She knew the mountains were there, and the rivers, and the cities, and the seas. She had seen them all in her mind.
"Thank you, wind," said Skye.
"Thank you for listening," said the wind.

That night, Skye hung on her hook with the white feather tucked safely in her ribbons. The wind tapped softly on the window, and Skye listened to one more story, until her stripes grew sleepy and she drifted off to dream of faraway places.

title: The Garden at Night
paragraphs: Everyone knew the garden during the day. The bees buzzed among the flowers. The butterflies floated over the daisies. The children watered the tomatoes and picked the beans. But very few people knew what happened in the garden at night.
When the sun went down and the porch light clicked off, the garden woke up in a whole new way.

First came the fireflies. One blinked near the roses. Then another blinked near the fence. Soon dozens of tiny lights were floating above the grass, blinking on and off, on and off, like they were talking to each other in a secret code.

Next came the toad. His name was Barnaby, and he lived under a flat stone by the cucumbers. Every evening, he hopped out to sit on his stone and sing. His song was deep and croaky, and it went like this: "Brrr-ump. Brrr-ump." It wasn't the prettiest song, but Barnaby sang it with his whole heart.

Then the moonflowers opened. All day long, they had been tightly closed, like tiny white umbrellas. But when the moon came up, they slowly unfolded, wide and round and glowing. They smelled sweet, like honey.
A soft, fuzzy moth came to visit the moonflowers. Her wings were pale green, with little spots that looked like eyes. She drifted from flower to flower, sipping their sweet nectar.
"Good evening, Barnaby," said the moth.
"Good evening, Luna," said the toad. "The moonflowers are lovely tonight."
"They are," agreed Luna. "But have you noticed? The little pumpkin vine looks sad."
Barnaby hopped over to look. In the corner of the garden, a small pumpkin vine drooped over the dry dirt. Its leaves were curled and tired.
"Nobody watered this corner today," said Barnaby. "The children must have missed it."
Luna fluttered her wings. "What can we do? We are too small to carry the watering can."
Barnaby thought hard. Then he looked up at the sky. A few soft clouds were drifting over the moon. "Maybe we can ask for help," he said.
So Barnaby began to sing again, louder than ever. "Brrr-ump! Brrr-ump!" The crickets joined in with their chirps. The fireflies blinked faster. Even the owl in the big oak tree gave a gentle hoot.
High above, the clouds seemed to listen. They gathered together, gray and puffy, right over the garden. And then, very softly, it began to rain.
It was a gentle rain, the kind that sounds like whispering. It pattered on the leaves. It filled the little dips in the dirt. It soaked the dry corner where the pumpkin vine was waiting.
Slowly, the vine's leaves uncurled. They lifted toward the sky, drinking in the cool water.
"Look!" said Luna. "It's feeling better already."
Barnaby smiled his wide toad smile. "Sometimes, when you can't do something by yourself, all you have to do is ask, and your friends will help."
The rain stopped as softly as it began. The clouds drifted away, and the moon came out again, brighter than before. Every leaf and petal in the garden sparkled with drops of water.
The next morning, the children came out to the garden. They found the pumpkin vine standing tall and green. In the middle of it, there was a tiny new flower, bright orange like the sunrise.
"It must have rained last night," said one of the children.

Under his flat stone, Barnaby the toad gave a sleepy little croak. He knew it was more than just rain. And that night, when the fireflies blinked and the moonflowers opened, the whole garden sang a quiet song of thanks.
